newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ENGLAND, FRANCE SEEK TO APPLY BRAKES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ENGLAND, FRANCE SEEK TO APPLY BRAKES.

text.p: England and France resume their battle for supremacy in northern hemisphere rugby on Saturday threatening to apply the brakes to the most free-scoring Five Nations season for years.

Whoever wins the showdown at Twickenham, where England have not lost to France for 10 years, will almost certainly be presented with the trophy on March 15, but there is no guarantee the action will be pretty.

England have scored 10 tries to France's eight in their two games to date, and the home side need just 32 more points in their remaining fixtures to establish a new pointscoring record for any team in Five Nations history.

Yet there is far less probability of France collapsing in the final quarter the way Scotland and Ireland did and this season's average of 5.5 tries per game may suffer if England, who have so far conceded only one themselves, follow orders.
"It is vital we play with control right from the start," said coach Jack Rowell, aware his team were wasteful in the first hour against both the Scots and Irish.
"The French have very good fluency and if we allow them to exhibit it, they can be frightening. We have to fence them in with our defensive play."

French counterpart Jean-Claude Skrela has been saying for months he is concerned by the strength of the English scrum, and the world's most capped player Philip Sella is among those who believe the performance of the French pack, rather than their speedy backs, will determine the outcome.

That would seem to indicate a fierce, tight encounter settled by isolated mistakes, reverting to the regular pattern of past Twickenham contests in which seven of the last nine Anglo-French tussles have been decided by four points or less.
England have the huge advantage of an unchanged side for the third match in a row, yet questions remain over their failure to burst into life earlier in a match.
Replacements Jeremy Guscott and Austin Healey were conspicuous late arrivals in the Irish game, and could be thrown into the action again if England's backline struggles for rhythm.

Skipper Phil de Glanville is still the subject of whispers about his place in the side since his omission from the 62-strong initial British Lions squad for the tour to South Africa, but his three tests in charge have so far yielded 54, 41 and 46 points respectively.

It helps explain why Rowell admires the Bath centre for his organisational qualities and, along with Jon Sleightholme and Tony Underwood, De Glanville still has time to force Lions manager Fran Cotton into a U-turn.
The French, who headed for a plush Knightsbridge hotel after arriving in London by Eurostar train on Thursday, simply want to shed their reputation as Five Nations underachievers.

They have collected only one title in the last seven years but are keen to extend the symmetrical sequence which has brought them outright championship success in 1967, 1977 and 1987. They have also beaten England in their last two meetings, at Parc des Princes last year and Loftus Versfeld, Pretoria, in the 1995 World Cup third place play-off.
